title: Topology and Bundle Theory — Glossary
description: Topological and bundle-theoretic vocabulary used in the multi-sheeted n-gon tiling project. Covers sheets, covers, holonomies, and gauge structures — the geometric infrastructure underlying reconnection.

manifold.summary: A locally Euclidean topological space where every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝⁿ.
manifold.definition:
A **locally Euclidean topological space** — every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some fixed $n$ (the manifold's dimension).

Examples:
- $\mathbb{R}^n$, $S^n$.
- Surfaces (2-manifolds): sphere, torus, hyperbolic plane.
- 3-manifolds: $\mathbb{R}^3$, $S^3$, Poincaré dodecahedral space.

examples.title: Euclidean space
examples.body: $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the simplest manifold of dimension $n$; every point has a neighborhood that is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

examples.title: Sphere
examples.body: $S^2$ is a 2-manifold: every point on the sphere has a neighborhood homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$ (a small disk).

examples.title: Torus
examples.body: The torus $T^2$ is a 2-manifold obtained by identifying opposite edges of a square. Locally it looks like $\mathbb{R}^2$.

cw-complex.summary: A topological space built inductively from cells (points, edges, disks, etc.) attached via specified maps.
cw-complex.definition: A topological space built **inductively from cells**: 0-cells (points), 1-cells (edges), 2-cells (disks), etc., attached via specified maps. Every tiling defines a CW complex structure on its ambient space.

examples.title: Tiling as CW complex
examples.body: A planar tiling defines a CW complex: vertices are 0-cells, edges are 1-cells, and tile interiors are 2-cells. The attaching maps specify how each cell's boundary connects to lower-dimensional cells.

examples.title: Sphere as CW complex
examples.body: $S^2$ can be given a CW structure with one 0-cell and one 2-cell, or with two 0-cells, one 1-cell, and two 2-cells (like a globe with north/south poles).

formulas.description: Euler characteristic as alternating sum of cell counts in a CW complex.

quotient-space.summary: A topological space obtained by identifying equivalent points under an equivalence relation.
quotient-space.definition:
The space obtained by **identifying equivalent points** under an equivalence relation.

Examples:
- $\mathbb{R}^n / \mathbb{Z}^n$ = torus $T^n$.
- $S^2 / \{\pm 1\}$ = projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$.
- Pentagon expansion family quotiented by translations = a quasiperiodic structure.

examples.title: Torus from the plane
examples.body: $\mathbb{R}^2 / \mathbb{Z}^2$ identifies points that differ by integer vectors, yielding the torus $T^2$. The square $[0,1]^2$ with opposite edges identified is a fundamental domain.

examples.title: Projective plane
examples.body: $S^2 / \{\pm 1\}$ identifies antipodal points on the sphere, yielding the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$.

examples.title: Quasiperiodic structure
examples.body: The pentagon expansion family quotiented by translations yields a quasiperiodic structure, encoding the self-similar nature of Penrose-type tilings.

punctured-plane.summary: The plane ℝ² with a discrete vortex set Σ removed; the base space of the pentagon's multi-sheeted bundle.
punctured-plane.definition:
The space $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Sigma$ for a **vortex set $\Sigma$** (a discrete set of points). Base space of the pentagon's multi-sheeted bundle: the punctures are the vertices around which sheet transitions accumulate.

The fundamental group of the punctured plane is the **free group** on $|\Sigma|$ generators (one loop around each puncture).

examples.title: Single puncture
examples.body: $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ has fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}$: loops are classified by their winding number around the removed point $p$.

examples.title: Multiple vortices
examples.body: $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p_1, \ldots, p_k\}$ has fundamental group $F_k$, the free group of rank $k$. Each generator corresponds to a loop encircling exactly one puncture.

formulas.description: Fundamental group of the plane with k punctures is the free group of rank k.

simply-connected.summary: A space with trivial fundamental group, meaning every loop is contractible.
simply-connected.definition:
Having **trivial fundamental group**: every loop is contractible. The plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is simply connected; the punctured plane is **not**.

Multi-sheeted covers exist precisely because the underlying base is **not** simply connected.

examples.title: Euclidean plane
examples.body: $\mathbb{R}^2$ is simply connected: any loop in the plane can be continuously shrunk to a point.

examples.title: Punctured plane is not simply connected
examples.body: $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ is not simply connected: a loop encircling the origin cannot be contracted to a point without crossing the removed point.

formulas.description: A space X is simply connected if and only if its fundamental group is trivial.

fundamental-group.summary: The group of homotopy classes of loops based at a fixed point, with operation given by loop concatenation.
fundamental-group.definition:
The **group of homotopy classes of loops** based at a fixed point. Operation: loop concatenation.

For our spaces:
- $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^n) = 1$ (trivial).
- $\pi_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$ (winding number).
- $\pi_1(T^2) = \mathbb{Z}^2$ (two independent loops).
- $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}) = \mathbb{Z}$ (encircling the puncture).
- $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p_1, \ldots, p_k\}) = F_k$ (free group of rank $k$).
- $\pi_1(SO(3)) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ (spinor doubling).

examples.title: Circle
examples.body: $\pi_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$: loops on the circle are classified by their winding number — how many times they wrap around.

examples.title: Torus
examples.body: $\pi_1(T^2) = \mathbb{Z}^2$: the torus has two independent non-contractible loops, one going around each handle.

examples.title: SO(3) and spinors
examples.body: $\pi_1(SO(3)) = \mathbb{Z}/2$: a rotation by $2\pi$ is not contractible, but a rotation by $4\pi$ is. This is the topological origin of spinor doubling.

formulas.description: Fundamental group of the plane with k punctures.
Fundamental group of the circle is the integers (winding number).

loops-homotopy.summary: Two loops are homotopic if one can be continuously deformed into the other; homotopy classes capture topological winding behavior.
loops-homotopy.definition: Two loops are **homotopic** if one can be continuously deformed into the other. The homotopy class of a loop captures its topological "winding behavior" — useful for detecting topological defects (vortices).

examples.title: Contractible loop
examples.body: A loop in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that does not encircle any puncture is homotopic to a constant loop (a point). Its homotopy class is trivial.

examples.title: Non-contractible loop around a vortex
examples.body: A loop encircling a vortex in $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ cannot be contracted to a point. Its homotopy class is a nonzero element of $\mathbb{Z}$, given by the winding number.

topological-defect.summary: A singularity that cannot be removed by local deformation; vortices are 2D topological defects.
topological-defect.definition: A **singularity that cannot be removed by local deformation**. Vortices are 2D topological defects: shrinking a loop around a vortex never makes it contractible while keeping it inside the punctured plane.

examples.title: Vortex in 2D
examples.body: A vortex at the origin of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a topological defect: any loop encircling the origin has nonzero winding number and cannot be contracted to a point in $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$.

examples.title: Pentagon vertex as defect
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted pentagon cover, each vertex of the tiling is a topological defect. Encircling a vertex once shifts the sheet by the $36°$ deficit angle, corresponding to a nontrivial element of $\mathbb{Z}/10$.

covering-space.summary: A continuous map π: ℳ → X that is a local homeomorphism, with X covered by open sets whose preimages are disjoint unions of homeomorphic copies (sheets).
covering-space.definition:
A continuous map $\pi: \mathcal{M} \to X$ that is a **local homeomorphism**, with $X$ covered by open sets $U$ where $\pi^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of copies of $U$ each mapped homeomorphically to $U$. Each copy is a **sheet**.

Properties:
- Number of sheets is constant on connected components of $X$ (assuming $X$ is locally connected).
- Covering spaces correspond bijectively to subgroups of $\pi_1(X)$.
- The **universal cover** is the unique simply connected covering space.

examples.title: Real line over the circle
examples.body: The map $\mathbb{R} \to S^1$ given by $t \mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$ is a covering map. The fiber over any point is a copy of $\mathbb{Z}$, and each small arc in $S^1$ lifts to infinitely many disjoint arcs in $\mathbb{R}$.

examples.title: Subgroup correspondence
examples.body: For $X = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Sigma$, covering spaces correspond to subgroups of $\pi_1(X) = F_{|\Sigma|}$. The $n$-sheeted cover corresponds to a subgroup of index $n$.

multi-sheeted-cover.summary: A covering space with multiple sheets, allowing tile-projection overlaps where distinct tiles project to overlapping regions.
multi-sheeted-cover.definition: A covering space with **multiple sheets** — i.e., $|\pi^{-1}(x)| > 1$ for some (hence all) regular $x \in X$. Allows tile-projection overlaps: two distinct tiles in $\mathcal{M}$ can project to overlapping regions of $X$.

examples.title: Pentagon multi-sheeted cover
examples.body: The multi-sheeted pentagon cover is a discrete combinatorial analogue of a Riemann surface with branch points of order 10. Sheets correspond to elements of $\mathbb{Z}/10$, and crossing an edge shifts the sheet by the associated deficit angle.

examples.title: Tile overlap via sheets
examples.body: Two tiles on different sheets of the cover can project to overlapping regions of the base plane. This is the mechanism by which the multi-sheeted structure encodes the quasicrystal's local matching rules.

universal-cover.summary: The unique simply connected covering space of a given space.
universal-cover.definition: The **unique simply connected covering space** of a given base space $X$. It corresponds to the trivial subgroup of $\pi_1(X)$ under the subgroup correspondence for covering spaces. Every other covering space of $X$ is a quotient of the universal cover.

examples.title: Universal cover of the circle
examples.body: The universal cover of $S^1$ is $\mathbb{R}$, via the map $t \mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$. The deck transformations are integer translations.

examples.title: Universal cover of the torus
examples.body: The universal cover of $T^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$ is $\mathbb{R}^2$, with deck transformations given by integer lattice translations.

double-cover.summary: A 2-fold covering space; canonical examples include SU(2) → SO(3) encoding spinor doubling.
double-cover.definition:
A **2-fold covering space**. The canonical examples:
- $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$.
- $SU(2) \to SO(3)$, encoding spinor doubling.
- $\text{Spin}(n) \to SO(n)$.

examples.title: SU(2) → SO(3)
examples.body: $SU(2)$ is the double cover of $SO(3)$: two elements $\pm A \in SU(2)$ map to the same rotation in $SO(3)$. This is the topological origin of spinors in quantum mechanics.

examples.title: Sphere over projective space
examples.body: $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ is the double cover identifying antipodal points. The fiber over each point of $\mathbb{RP}^n$ consists of two antipodal points of $S^n$.

branched-cover.summary: A covering with ramification points where the local homeomorphism property fails; sheets collapse above branch points.
branched-cover.definition:
A covering with **ramification points** where the local homeomorphism property fails. Above a branch point, sheets "collapse" — typically $\pi$ is locally $z \mapsto z^k$ for some $k > 1$.

In our setting: the multi-sheeted pentagon cover is branched at **vertex points** of the tiling. Encircling a vertex once shifts the sheet by the deficit angle.

examples.title: Complex power map
examples.body: The map $w = z^n$ defines an $n$-sheeted branched cover of $\mathbb{C}$ over $\mathbb{C}$, branched at $z = 0$. Near the origin, $n$ sheets collapse to one.

examples.title: Pentagon vertex branching
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted pentagon cover, each vertex is a branch point of order 10. Encircling a vertex once shifts the sheet by $36°$ (one step in $\mathbb{Z}/10$), and going around 10 times returns to the original sheet.

formulas.description: Local model of a branched cover near a branch point of order k.

branch-point.summary: A point of the base space above which the covering fails to be a local homeomorphism; the fiber has fewer elements than over generic points.
branch-point.definition: A point of the base space above which the covering fails to be a local homeomorphism. The fiber above a branch point has fewer elements than over generic points.

examples.title: Origin under z²
examples.body: For the map $z \mapsto z^2$, the origin is a branch point: the fiber over $0$ is just $\{0\}$, while the fiber over any nonzero point has two elements.

examples.title: Tiling vertex
examples.body: In the pentagon multi-sheeted cover, each tiling vertex is a branch point. The angular deficit of $36°$ per vertex means sheets merge at these points.

riemann-surface.summary: A complex 1-manifold (2-manifold with complex analytic structure); the classical setting for branched covers.
riemann-surface.definition:
A **complex 1-manifold**, i.e., a 2-manifold equipped with complex analytic structure. Classical setting for branched covers: $w = z^{1/n}$ defines an $n$-sheeted Riemann surface over $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$.

The pentagon multi-sheeted cover is the **discrete combinatorial analogue** of a Riemann surface with branch points of order 10.

examples.title: Riemann surface of z^(1/n)
examples.body: The function $w = z^{1/n}$ is multi-valued on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. Its Riemann surface is an $n$-sheeted cover of $\mathbb{C}$, branched at $0$ and $\infty$.

examples.title: Pentagon cover as discrete Riemann surface
examples.body: The multi-sheeted pentagon cover is the discrete combinatorial analogue of a Riemann surface with branch points of order 10, one at each tiling vertex.

physical-space.summary: The subspace of the cut-and-project ambient lattice containing the actual quasicrystal; for Penrose tiling, 2-dimensional inside ℝ⁵.
physical-space.definition: The **subspace of cut-and-project ambient lattice** containing the actual quasicrystal. For Penrose tiling, $\dim E_\parallel = 2$ inside $\mathbb{R}^5$.

examples.title: Penrose tiling
examples.body: For the Penrose tiling, $E_\parallel$ is a 2-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^5$ with an irrational slope with respect to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^5$.

perpendicular-space.summary: The orthogonal complement of the physical space in the ambient lattice; hosts the acceptance window.
perpendicular-space.definition: The **orthogonal complement** of $E_\parallel$ in the ambient lattice. Hosts the acceptance window. For Penrose, $\dim E_\perp = 3$.

examples.title: Penrose tiling
examples.body: For the Penrose tiling, $E_\perp$ is 3-dimensional inside $\mathbb{R}^5$. The acceptance window is a pentagonal region in $E_\perp$.

acceptance-window.summary: The bounded region in perpendicular space filtering which lattice points project to the physical tiling.
acceptance-window.definition:
The **bounded region in $E_\perp$** filtering which lattice points project to the physical tiling.

Window shape determines the resulting tiling combinatorics:
- Pentagonal window: Penrose tiling.
- Triacontahedral window: AKN tiling.
- Octagonal window: Ammann–Beenker tiling.

examples.title: Pentagonal window → Penrose tiling
examples.body: Using a regular pentagonal acceptance window in $E_\perp$ selects exactly those lattice points whose projections form a Penrose tiling in $E_\parallel$.

examples.title: Octagonal window → Ammann–Beenker tiling
examples.body: An octagonal acceptance window yields the Ammann–Beenker tiling, an 8-fold symmetric quasicrystal.

connection.summary: A rule for parallel transport in a fiber bundle; in smooth geometry, a connection 1-form valued in the Lie algebra of the structure group.
connection.definition: A rule for **parallel transport** in a fiber bundle. In smooth differential geometry: a connection 1-form valued in the Lie algebra of the structure group. In discrete settings, see **Discrete Connection**.

examples.title: Levi-Civita connection
examples.body: On a Riemannian manifold, the Levi-Civita connection provides parallel transport of tangent vectors along curves, preserving the metric.

examples.title: Gauge field in physics
examples.body: In Yang–Mills theory, the gauge field $A_\mu$ is a connection 1-form on a principal $G$-bundle over spacetime. The field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ is its curvature.

discrete-connection.summary: An assignment of group elements to edges of a CW complex; the discrete analogue of a smooth connection.
discrete-connection.definition: An **assignment of group elements to edges** of a CW complex. In a lattice gauge theory, each edge $e$ carries a group element $g_e \in G$. Composition along a path gives parallel transport. The framework's **sheet transitions** $\tau(e)$ are exactly this kind of discrete connection.

examples.title: Sheet transitions as discrete connection
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted pentagon cover, each edge $e$ of the tiling carries a group element $\tau(e) \in \mathbb{Z}/10$ specifying the sheet change when crossing that edge. This is a discrete connection on the tiling's CW complex.

examples.title: Lattice gauge theory

parallel-transport.summary: Transport of fiber elements along paths via a connection; in discrete settings, walking along a path multiplies the group elements on the edges.
parallel-transport.definition: **Transport of fiber elements along paths via a connection**. In a discrete setting: walking along a path multiplies the group elements on the edges.

examples.title: Parallel transport on a sphere
examples.body: Transporting a tangent vector around a closed loop on $S^2$ rotates it by an angle equal to the solid angle enclosed by the loop — a nontrivial holonomy.

examples.title: Discrete path product
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted tiling, parallel transport along a path $e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n$ gives the product $\tau(e_1) \cdot \tau(e_2) \cdots \tau(e_n) \in \mathbb{Z}/10$.

holonomy.summary: The group element accumulated by parallel transport around a closed loop; nontrivial holonomy detects curvature or monodromy.
holonomy.definition: The **group element accumulated by parallel transport around a closed loop**. For a trivial connection, holonomy is identity for all loops. Nontrivial holonomy detects **curvature** (smooth case) or **monodromy** (discrete case).

examples.title: Holonomy on a sphere
examples.body: Parallel transporting a tangent vector around a spherical triangle returns it rotated by the triangle's spherical excess. This is the holonomy of the Levi-Civita connection.

examples.title: Holonomy around a vortex
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted pentagon cover, the holonomy of a small loop around a vortex equals $1 \in \mathbb{Z}/10$ (one step, corresponding to $36°$). This is the concentrated curvature at each vertex.

monodromy.summary: The holonomy of a closed loop in a covering or bundle; for the pentagon cover, the monodromy around a vortex equals the 36° deficit angle in ℤ/10.
monodromy.definition: The **holonomy of a closed loop** in a covering or bundle. For the pentagon cover, the monodromy of a small loop around a vortex equals the deficit angle ($36°$) in the fiber group $\mathbb{Z}/10$.

examples.title: Monodromy of z^(1/n)
examples.body: For the function $w = z^{1/n}$, transporting a branch around the origin once multiplies $w$ by $e^{2\pi i/n}$. This is the monodromy of the $n$-sheeted cover.

examples.title: Pentagon vertex monodromy
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted pentagon cover, the monodromy of a loop encircling one vertex is $1 \in \mathbb{Z}/10$, corresponding to a $36°$ sheet shift. Going around 10 times gives trivial monodromy.

formulas.description: Holonomy representation: maps loops in the punctured plane to group elements, classifying the cover up to isomorphism.

transition-function.summary: The map between trivializations of a fiber bundle, valued in the structure group; in the discrete pinwheel setting, these are sheet-change maps assigned to each edge.
transition-function.definition: The **map between trivializations** of a fiber bundle, valued in the structure group. In the discrete pinwheel setting, transition functions are **sheet-change maps assigned to each edge** — the same thing as the discrete connection's edge labels $\tau(e)$.

examples.title: Möbius band
examples.body: The Möbius band is a line bundle over $S^1$ with a single nontrivial transition function: the map $x \mapsto -x$ on the fiber $\mathbb{R}$, applied where the two trivializing patches overlap.

examples.title: Sheet-change maps
examples.body: In the multi-sheeted pentagon cover, the transition function on edge $e$ is $\tau(e) \in \mathbb{Z}/10$, specifying how the sheet label changes when crossing $e$.

principal-bundle.summary: A fiber bundle with G-action where fibers are copies of G and transitions preserve the G-structure.
principal-bundle.definition:
A **fiber bundle with $G$-action** — fibers are copies of $G$, transitions and bundle operations preserve $G$-structure.

Smooth example: the orthonormal frame bundle of a Riemannian manifold ($G = O(n)$).

examples.title: Frame bundle
examples.body: The orthonormal frame bundle of a Riemannian $n$-manifold is a principal $O(n)$-bundle. A point in the fiber over $x$ is an orthonormal basis for the tangent space $T_x M$.

examples.title: Gauge theory
examples.body: In Yang–Mills theory, the gauge field lives on a principal $G$-bundle over spacetime. Gauge transformations are automorphisms of this bundle.

discrete-principal-bundle.summary: The combinatorial analogue of a principal G-bundle: a CW complex with sheet labels in G and edges assigned G-elements determining sheet transformations.
discrete-principal-bundle.definition:
The **combinatorial analogue**: a CW complex whose 0-cells carry sheet labels in $G$, with edges assigned $G$-elements (the discrete connection) that determine how sheet labels transform when crossing.

This is the precise structure of the **multi-sheeted pinwheel cover**.

examples.title: Multi-sheeted pinwheel cover
examples.body: The multi-sheeted pinwheel cover is a discrete principal $\mathbb{Z}/10$-bundle over the tiling's CW complex. Each vertex carries a sheet label in $\mathbb{Z}/10$, and each edge carries a group element specifying the sheet change.

local-finiteness.summary: The condition that every compact region contains finitely many tiles; fundamental for any reasonable tiling.
local-finiteness.definition:
The **finiteness condition**: every compact region contains finitely many tiles. A fundamental requirement for any reasonable tiling.

Failed when irrational rotation orbits densify the plane (cyclotomic density trap). Restored by either:
- Restricting to rational rotations (orientation group finite).
- Using cut-and-project (acceptance window bounded).

examples.title: Penrose tiling
examples.body: The Penrose tiling is locally finite: any bounded region of the plane contains only finitely many tiles, even though the tiling is aperiodic.

examples.title: Cyclotomic density trap
examples.body: If irrational rotations are allowed without restriction, the orbit of a single tile under the rotation group can densify the plane, violating local finiteness.

euler-characteristic.summary: The alternating sum of cell counts in a CW complex; related to total Gaussian curvature via the Gauss–Bonnet theorem.
euler-characteristic.definition:
The **alternating sum of cell counts** in a CW complex:

$$\chi = c_0 - c_1 + c_2 - c_3 + \cdots$$

For a closed surface: $\chi = v - e + f$.

Key values:
- Sphere $S^2$: $\chi = 2$.
- Torus $T^2$: $\chi = 0$.
- Genus-$g$ surface: $\chi = 2 - 2g$.

**Gauss–Bonnet theorem** relates $\chi$ to total Gaussian curvature, linking topology to geometry. Pentagonal frustration's $36°$ deficit per vertex shows up via Gauss–Bonnet when interpreting the multi-sheeted cover as a polyhedral surface.

examples.title: Sphere
examples.body: For a tetrahedron (homeomorphic to $S^2$): $v = 4$, $e = 6$, $f = 4$, so $\chi = 4 - 6 + 4 = 2$.

examples.title: Torus
examples.body: The torus has $\chi = 0$. A CW structure with 1 vertex, 2 edges, and 1 face gives $\chi = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$.

examples.title: Gauss–Bonnet and pentagonal deficit
examples.body: The $36°$ angular deficit per vertex of the pentagon tiling contributes to the total curvature. By Gauss–Bonnet, the sum of all deficits equals $2\pi \chi$, providing a topological accounting of angular shortfalls.

formulas.description: Euler characteristic as alternating sum of cell counts.
Euler characteristic for a closed surface in terms of vertices, edges, and faces.
Euler characteristic of a closed orientable surface of genus g.
Gauss–Bonnet theorem: total Gaussian curvature equals 2π times the Euler characteristic.
